e.t: Abaran, also given as Avaran, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 6:59. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s role or significance.

Abitōb, also rendered Avitov, is a personal name, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament tradition, it identifies one individual and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:11. Because the available record gives the name but no verse text or wider context, its precise significance in that genealogy cannot be explained further here. The safest reading is simply the person’s name.

The word means “Hades,” the name used for the realm associated with the dead. It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical writings. This LXX word occurs 95 times across 92 verses, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Song of Songs. Its use appears especially often in Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Sirach, and Job. The precise force of the word in any individual verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

This proper name identifies Aiin, also rendered “In.” It is a named entity rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 18:23. The available wording supports recognizing it as a name, while the reference alone does not provide enough context to explain more about the place or person it identifies.

Akkaron is a proper name for a place known in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with an ordinary action or quality; its role is to identify a location. The name appears 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek Deuterocanonical corpus, beginning in Joshua and continuing into 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and account.

This Greek LXX verb means “compel”: to make someone do something through pressure or authority. It describes an action directed toward another person, rather than a feeling or simple suggestion. The word appears 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including Proverbs and several passages in the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This proper name identifies an “Anathōthitēs,” also rendered “Anathothitis.” It is a personal or group designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 23:27. The available lexical wording identifies the name, but does not provide additional detail about the person’s role or the significance of the designation in that verse.

Ananeēl, also rendered Ananil, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word or action; its function is simply as a personal designation. The name occurs three times in this corpus: twice in Nehemiah and once in Zechariah. Its precise reference in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This verb means “blocked up”—to close off an opening or passage so that movement through it is stopped. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament data, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 4:1. The word’s basic idea is physical obstruction: something is shut, filled, or sealed so that access is prevented. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “taken in return” or “deducted.” It describes an amount being taken back or subtracted rather than simply given or added. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 27:18. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself emphasizes a reduction made by taking something away or accounting for it in return. This is an action word describing what happens to an amount or value.

Antiocheia, also rendered Antiokhia, is a proper name for the city of Antioch. It identifies a place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus represented here, the name occurs 14 times, appearing in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding account, but the word itself functions simply as a place-name.

This word means “storehouse,” a place where goods, provisions, or valuable things are kept. It is a noun describing a storage room, building, or enclosed place rather than the things stored there. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, including passages about Israel’s provisions, blessings and curses connected with a person’s storehouses, and the planned rooms of the temple. Its basic sense remains consistent: a designated place for keeping supplies or possessions.

This word means “recourse”: something a person turns to for help, support, or relief. As a noun, it names the resort or appeal itself rather than the action of turning. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears 19 times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains recourse—a place, person, or means to which one looks when help or resolution is needed.

This verb means “pronounce”: it describes the act of expressing words or a message aloud. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, so it is uncommon but used across several books. Its exact force in any individual passage depends on what is being pronounced and the surrounding verse, which are not available here. The central idea remains spoken expression—someone pronouncing words, rather than merely holding them in thought.

Asiel, also rendered Asil, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals mentioned in genealogical and administrative passages rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs five times in the LXX corpus, in Genesis, Numbers, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from the person and surrounding context named there.

This adjective describes something refined and pure—clean, unmixed, and suitable in its intended use. It presents the quality of an object rather than naming a person, action, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 27:20, and is rendered “refined.” The central idea is purity produced by removing what is unwanted, leaving something clean and fit for use.

This adjective means “without light,” describing something lacking illumination. It is a Greek LXX word with a straightforward descriptive function: it identifies a person, place, object, or condition as dark or unlit, without itself explaining the reason for that darkness. The word occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Wisdom 17:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This word means “chaff,” the light, dry material separated from grain after harvesting. It is a noun naming an agricultural byproduct rather than the useful grain itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times across 20 verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Isaiah, and Job. Its basic meaning remains concrete: the husks or worthless material removed from grain. When the word appears figuratively, its meaning depends on the surrounding passage, but the underlying picture is still something light and discarded in contrast with what is valuable.

Badan, also rendered Vathan, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:17, identifying a person in a genealogy. The name itself supplies the person’s designation; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s family connection or historical role. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name Badan or Vathan.

This word is a proper name, preserved in the forms “Balegdae” and “Valegthae.” It identifies a specific named individual or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 14:7. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise referent cannot be described further, but its lexical function is that of a personal name recorded in the biblical genealogy or historical record.

This verb describes speech or sound as “of barbarous; outlandish sound”—something perceived as foreign, strange, or unintelligible to the hearer. It does not by itself describe a person’s character; its focus is the quality of the sound or speech. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 13:9. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how the word functions there.

Beor is a proper name, rendered “Beōr” or “Veor,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 11 verses, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 1 Chronicles, Job, and Micah. The name appears in references connected with people identified as Beor. Its specific significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its immediate context.

This LXX noun means “noose”: a loop or snare used to catch or hold someone. It names a concrete means of entrapment rather than an action or character trait. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek Deuterocanonical text represented here—three times in Proverbs and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “taste” or “eat”: it describes taking food into the mouth, whether sampling it or consuming it. The wording can therefore refer to the act of eating generally or to experiencing a particular taste, depending on the sentence. It occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including uses rendered “taste” and “eat.” Its precise emphasis in any verse comes from the surrounding context.

This noun means “gloom”: a condition of deep darkness, dimness, or obscurity. It names darkness as an enveloping condition rather than an action or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 27 times, chiefly in the Old Testament books, including passages in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, Isaiah, and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains gloom or deep darkness.

Gola is a proper name used for a person or place in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying name. The name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from Genesis, Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage and the person or location being named.

This noun means “discrimination; distinction”: the act or quality of recognizing that one thing differs from another. It expresses discernment or separation between things, rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Job 37:16. That reference identifies its location, while the word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “ransack”: to search through a place forcefully and thoroughly, often while taking what is found. It describes an active act of plundering rather than a quiet search. The word appears 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it can describe repeated or widespread acts of seizure across different passages. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being searched, seized, or plundered in the surrounding context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “cut in two,” describing the act of dividing something into two parts. It is a specific action word rather than a general term for cutting. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 29:17, so its normal meaning is clear even though its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated occurrences. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to one who takes bribes: a person who accepts money or gifts in exchange for improper favor. It identifies the kind of person being described rather than an action, object, or place. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 15:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: someone characterized by taking bribes.

This Greek LXX preposition means “into” or “for.” It commonly marks movement toward or entry into something, and it can also identify the purpose or intended recipient of an action. The word is very frequent in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, occurring 7,244 times, so its precise sense depends on the words and situation around it. It appears from Genesis through Song of Songs, including uses rendered “into” in Deuteronomy 29:12 and 1 Samuel 2:14.

This word means “implementation”—the carrying out or putting into effect of something planned, required, or established. As a noun, it refers to the completed or unfolding action of making something real in practice, rather than merely discussing or intending it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:14; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “from within,” describing something that comes from or is located inside. As an adverb, it tells where something originates or is situated, emphasizing an inner source or position. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, appearing once in Numbers, once in Wisdom, and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines its precise force in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX word means “ninety years old.” It is an age word, used to describe a person who has reached ninety years of age. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:24. The word itself identifies the person’s age; the surrounding passage is needed to understand the particular situation in which that age is mentioned.

This adjective means “dislocated”: it describes something moved out of its normal position, especially a bodily part whose proper alignment has been disturbed. It functions as a describing word rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:13. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

Correction means the act of setting something right or putting it back into proper condition. It is a noun describing this restoring or rectifying action, rather than the person who performs it. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 14:34. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This adjective means “gained besides”: it describes something acquired in addition to what was already possessed or present. It points to an added acquisition rather than the original thing itself, so its meaning is relational—it depends on what has already been gained or held. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 6:23; the surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what was added there.

This adjective describes something marked by seven towers or possessing seven towers. It is a descriptive word, identifying a structure by the number of its towers rather than naming the structure itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:7. The reference identifies where the word appears, but the precise force of the description depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means a “prop” or “stay”: something that supports, steadies, or holds another thing in place. Its central idea is dependable support rather than movement or change. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 14:26. Because only the reference is available without the verse text, its precise force there depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a supporting aid or brace.

Esthemon is a proper name, referring to a person named Esthemon rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:17. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself supplies the identification, while the passage provides the details about who this person was and how he fits into the account.

This adjective means “easily moved.” It describes something readily shifted from one place or position to another, emphasizing its lack of resistance to movement. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX material preserved here, both times in Wisdom: once in Wisdom 7:22 and once in Wisdom 13:11. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and what is being described.

Eupolemos is a proper name referring to a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 8:17 and 2 Maccabees 4:11. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish the person’s role or significance in either passage. Its basic function is simply to identify someone named Eupolemos.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Zaithan” or “Zethan.” It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:10. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its role as a personal designation; the available information does not provide an additional definition or explain the name’s underlying significance. Its precise reference in that passage belongs to the surrounding genealogical context.

Ēliatha, also rendered Iliatha, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 25:4. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide a separate definition or verse text, its ordinary function is simply to identify a person in that passage. Its precise significance there must be understood from the surrounding account of 1 Chronicles 25.

This noun means “foundation”: the supporting base on which something is established or built. It names the beginning or underlying support of a structure rather than the structure itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Joshua and Ezra. Its meaning remains focused and concrete, though the surrounding verse determines what is being founded. The word is rendered “foundation” in the available Ezra occurrences.

This word means “lament”: an expressed cry of grief or mourning. As a noun, it names the sorrowful expression itself rather than the person who mourns or the event causing grief. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 30 times, showing repeated use for formal or audible expressions of sorrow. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a lament over loss, distress, or judgment.

This noun means “healer,” referring to a person whose work is to bring healing. It identifies someone in the role of attending to sickness, rather than describing the healing action itself. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 11 times, making it a recurring but focused word for a person associated with healing. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This word is a proper name rendered “Ieous” or “Ieus.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Genesis 36. Because the available wording gives only the name itself and no description of the person, its basic meaning is simply this personal designation; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the individual more precisely.

This adverb means “cheerfully,” describing the manner in which someone performs an action. It presents the action as done in a positive, willing, and glad manner rather than reluctantly or sadly. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Job 22:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to describe the cheerful manner accompanying an action.

This word is a proper name referring to Josias, also rendered Iosias. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 33 times, chiefly in 2 Chronicles and 2 Kings, with additional occurrences in 1 Kings, Zechariah, and Sirach. The precise role of the person named depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “covering”: something that covers or serves as a cover. It names a covering rather than an action, so it refers to the object or layer that lies over something else. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 2:8. Its precise reference in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical sense remains a covering.

This adjective describes something made of tin, identifying its material rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 4:10. Its basic meaning is straightforward: the object or thing being described consists of tin. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what particular object it describes and why that object matters there; the word itself contributes the material description. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation corpus.

This Greek word means “kill” or “slay.” It is a verb describing the act of putting someone to death. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains direct and severe; the surrounding passage determines who is being killed and why. One occurrence is rendered “slay,” which agrees with the word’s central sense.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “throw stones at.” It describes the physical act of hurling stones toward someone, and its verb form presents that action as something being done. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Exodus and once in Numbers. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in either passage must be understood from its immediate context. Its basic meaning remains direct: attacking or attempting to strike someone with thrown stones.

This Greek LXX noun means “state” or “disposition,” referring to a person’s condition or settled manner. It describes how someone is situated or characterized rather than an action they perform. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:45. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense points to a condition, posture, or prevailing disposition.

This noun means “refuge” or “place of refuge”: a location or shelter to which someone flees for safety and protection. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for both physical places of safety and refuge understood in relation to God. The word occurs 23 times in the LXX corpus, including laws concerning cities of refuge and passages in Psalms that speak of taking refuge. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “bowl,” referring to a rounded vessel used to hold something. It is a noun, so it names the object rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezra 1:10. The word’s basic meaning is therefore straightforward: a bowl or similar container. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain what kind of bowl is intended or how it is being used there.

This Greek LXX verb means “swing” or “wave,” describing the movement of something back and forth. It can refer to an object or instrument being moved, or to a person making a waving motion. The word appears twice in the Greek text of the deuterocanonical books, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on what is being moved and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains active back-and-forth motion rather than a fixed position.

This adjective describes something intended or suitable for liturgical use—that is, for service connected with worship. It identifies a purpose or function rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, at 1 Chronicles 28:13. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but its basic sense remains something designated for use in worship or sacred service.

Maalath is a proper name, used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is the personal name itself rather than a translated concept. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Kings 4:16. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person and explain the name’s role in that passage.

This is a proper name identifying “Madianitōn,” also rendered “Mathianiton.” It functions as a name rather than a descriptive word, so its meaning is primarily the identity it names. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 31:2. The available lexical information does not provide a broader abstract meaning or additional usage pattern, so the safest understanding is that this word designates the named group or people associated with that name in the passage.

This LXX Greek verb means “dispose differently; correct.” It describes an action of changing how something is arranged or set in order, bringing it into a different or proper arrangement. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament collection, in Wisdom 19:18. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains an active change in arrangement or condition rather than a mere observation.

Melchēl, also rendered Melkhil, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament, and its precise significance cannot be established from the available lexical information alone. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 8:35. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s family connection or role there; the name itself functions simply as a personal designation.

This Greek LXX verb means “remove”: to take someone or something away from a place or position. As a verb, it describes an act of removal rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel and Psalms. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This noun means “bloodguiltiness”—culpability connected with the shedding of blood. It names the condition of being guilty for bloodshed rather than describing an action, person, or place. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but the central idea remains guilt associated with bloodshed. The word appears in 4 Maccabees 9:9 and 10:11.

Nabau, also rendered Navav, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal or place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. The exact person or location identified depends on the verse where it appears. This name occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and 1 Chronicles.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Nōbai” or “Nove.” It identifies a person or place by name rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 10:20. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s specific referent in that passage cannot be clarified further. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal or place-name “Nōbai; Nove.”

This Greek LXX noun means “wailing,” referring to an audible expression of deep grief or sorrow. It names the mournful cry itself rather than the person who cries. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus: once in Jeremiah and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central sense remains a voiced lament or expression of mourning.

This Greek LXX noun means “mercy” or “compassion”—a tender response toward someone who needs help or kindness. It names the quality or feeling of showing pity rather than describing an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 38:3, and its English rendering there is “compassion.” The word’s central idea is therefore a merciful concern directed toward another person. The surrounding verse supplies the specific force of the term in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “name”: to give someone or something a name, or to identify it by name. It describes the act of naming rather than the name itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 22 times, appearing in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its use can concern people, places, groups, or other things that are identified through a name. The surrounding passage determines whether the naming emphasizes simple identification or the act of assigning a name.

This adverb means “where.” It points to a place or location and helps connect an action, person, or statement with the place associated with it. In ordinary reading, it answers the question “where?” rather than naming the place itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:38. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic function remains a reference to location.

This adverb means “from the sky,” describing the direction or source from which something comes. It points upward to the sky as the place of origin, rather than naming an object or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 4:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

This adjective means “by the seaside,” describing something located beside or near the sea. It identifies a coastal setting rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including descriptions of places associated with the coast. Its precise reference in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a location beside the sea.

This Greek LXX verb means “deceive,” naming an action in which one person misleads another. It functions as a verb, so it describes what someone does rather than identifying a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Genesis 31:7. Its basic sense remains focused on deceptive action; the precise force of that action in the verse depends on the surrounding passage and its wording.

This word means “poor,” describing a condition of lacking material resources rather than having abundance. As a verb, it expresses being in a state of poverty, so it focuses on a person’s economic condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 30:9. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains straightforward: poverty or insufficient means. It does not by itself describe a person’s character, faith, or moral worth.

This Greek LXX verb means “fly”: to move through the air. It describes the action of flying rather than a person, creature, or object itself. The word appears 17 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 17 verses, so its basic meaning is used in several settings involving movement through the air. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “floodtide”: a powerful rise or surge of water. It refers to floodwater as it swells and moves forcefully, rather than to an ordinary stream or gentle flow. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 40:23. The word’s basic sense is therefore specific and concrete—an advancing floodtide. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This verb means “pre-exist”: to be present or happen before another person, thing, or event. It describes something already in place before a later point of reference, rather than something beginning at that moment. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs three times, in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what earlier or later subject the surrounding passage identifies.

This noun means “pillow,” a cushion used to support the head or body while resting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel 13:18 and 13:20. The word identifies an ordinary household object rather than an abstract idea or action. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a pillow or resting cushion. The repeated references in this short section show the word being used in a concrete, physical sense.

This verb means “pour to”: it describes liquid being poured toward or onto a person, place, or object. It is an action word, focusing on the direction of the pouring rather than merely on the liquid itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 23 times, especially in descriptions involving offerings and sacred procedures. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being poured and where it is directed.

Rabbath is a proper name for a place, rendered as “Rabbath” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a city mentioned in accounts involving David’s campaigns and in later prophetic passages. This name occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, across 2 Samuel, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. The word itself names the place rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition; its specific significance in any passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “latticework,” referring to a patterned framework made with crossed or arranged strips. It is a noun describing a physical architectural feature rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both occurrences appearing in 2 Kings 25:17. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the particular object and its role there, but the word itself points to an open, structured screen or framework.

Sebegōn, also given as Sevegon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a personal designation in the Greek Old Testament, appearing eight times across seven verses. Its occurrences are concentrated in genealogical lists in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, so its meaning is chiefly the identity of the person named, not an abstract idea or general description.

This adjective describes someone who is hard-hearted and stubborn—firmly resistant rather than willing to listen or respond. It portrays an inner attitude of resistance, not merely a brief moment of disagreement. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, so its central sense is clear even though it is uncommon. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This LXX noun means “groaning”: an audible expression of pain, weariness, or deep distress. It describes the sound or utterance that comes from someone carrying a heavy burden or suffering. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring description of human anguish and troubled prayer.
